h1: Are DoorDash and Uber Eats Worth It for Your Restaurant?
metaTitle: Is DoorDash Worth It for Restaurants? Honest Guide
metaDescription: Is DoorDash worth it for restaurants? An honest, plain breakdown of Uber Eats and DoorDash commissions, the real pros and cons, and how to make delivery pay.
heroAlt: A delivery courier picking up takeout bags at a restaurant counter
directAnswer: DoorDash and Uber Eats can be worth it, but only if you treat them as paid marketing, not free money. They take roughly 15 to 30 percent commission on each delivery order, plus payment processing and any ads you buy, so a busy night can still lose money if your prices and packaging are not built for it. They are worth it when you use them to reach new customers you could not reach on your own, price your delivery menu to protect your margin, and steadily nudge those customers toward ordering directly from you. They are not worth it if you lean on them as your main sales channel and let the fees quietly eat your profit.
keyTakeaways: The apps charge commission on every delivery order, roughly 15 to 30 percent depending on the plan you pick, plus card processing and any optional ads. Pickup orders cost less, usually around 6 to 10 percent.
The real upside is reach. You get in front of hungry people searching the app who would never have found you, and you skip the cost and headache of hiring your own delivery drivers.

The real downside is your margin and your data. After fees, delivery orders make far less than dine-in, and the app owns the customer, so you do not get their name, email, or phone to bring them back yourself.

Decide with simple math, not vibes. Know your food cost and your true profit on a typical order before and after a 30 percent cut. If delivery only works at a loss, it is a marketing cost, so treat it like one.
Make it profitable on purpose: set delivery menu prices higher than dine-in, invest in packaging that travels, turn on lower-cost pickup, and use the apps' free tools before their paid boosts.
Use the apps to get discovered, then win the repeat order on your own commission-free ordering, so the second and third visits keep the full amount instead of paying a fee every time.
intro:
It is a Friday night and your kitchen is slammed. Half the tickets on the rail are delivery orders from DoorDash and Uber Eats, so business looks great. Then the monthly statement lands, you see how much the apps kept, and your stomach drops. All those orders, and somehow the profit is not there.

If that sounds familiar, you are not doing anything wrong and you are not alone. Third-party delivery apps (the marketplaces like DoorDash and Uber Eats where customers browse restaurants, order, and get food dropped at their door) are one of the most confusing money decisions a restaurant owner faces today. They can genuinely grow your business, or they can quietly bleed it, and the difference comes down to how you use them.

This guide breaks it all down in plain language: how the fees actually work, the honest pros and cons, how to decide if they make sense for your spot, and the practical moves that turn delivery from a loss into a real channel. No hype, no scare tactics, just the math and the plan.

sections.h2: What is third-party delivery, and why does it feel like a trap?
sections.html:
Let us define the thing first. Third-party delivery means an outside company (a marketplace app like DoorDash, Uber Eats, or Grubhub) lists your restaurant, takes the customer's order, sends a driver to pick it up, and drops it at their door. You cook. They handle the app, the driver, and the payment. In exchange, they keep a cut of every order.

It feels like a trap for one simple reason: the orders look like pure upside, but the cost is hidden in a statement you only see later. A dine-in guest who spends 40 dollars leaves you close to 40 dollars, minus food and labor. That same 40 dollar order on an app might leave you 28 dollars before you have even paid for the food. Same work in the kitchen, very different profit.

None of that makes the apps bad. It makes them a paid channel, like an ad. The owners who win with delivery are the ones who understand exactly what they are paying and make sure each order still earns its keep. The owners who struggle are the ones who treat delivery like free extra business and never do the math. This guide keeps you in the first group.

sections.h2: How does the commission model actually work?
sections.html:
Here is the part nobody explains clearly. When you sign up, the apps do not charge one flat fee. They offer tiered plans, and the plan you choose sets your commission (the percentage of each order they keep).

  • DoorDash offers plans that run roughly from 15 percent (basic) up to 25 to 30 percent (their higher tiers, which promise more visibility in the app). Pickup orders, where the customer comes to get the food, cost much less, around 6 percent.
  • Uber Eats works the same way, with delivery plans that land in about the same 15 to 30 percent range and a lower pickup rate of roughly 6 to 10 percent.

The commission is only the headline number. On top of it, expect:

  1. Payment processing. A card fee of roughly 2.5 to 3.5 percent is often added, the same kind of fee your regular card reader charges.
  2. Optional ads and promotions. The apps constantly push you to buy "sponsored" placement or run discounts. These are optional, but if you use them, your real cost on those orders can climb toward 30 to 35 percent or more.

Here is a simple example, an illustration and not a promise. Say a customer orders 40 dollars of food on a 30 percent plan. The app keeps about 12 dollars, leaving you roughly 28. Out of that you still pay for the ingredients, the cook, the packaging, and the electricity. If your food cost is around 12 dollars, you can see how thin the leftover slice gets. That is the whole game: knowing that slice before the orders start rolling in.

sections.h2: What are the real upsides of being on the apps?
sections.html:
The fees are real, but so are the benefits, and it is not fair to look at only one side. Here is what you are actually buying.

  • Reach you cannot get on your own. Millions of people open DoorDash and Uber Eats when they are hungry and have not decided where to eat. Being listed puts you in front of them at the exact moment they are ready to spend. For a new or unknown spot, this is real discovery you would otherwise pay an ad agency for.
  • No delivery staff to hire or manage. Running your own drivers means insurance, wages, cars, no-shows, and liability if someone crashes. The apps absorb all of that. You never touch a delivery car.
  • Orders during your slow hours. Delivery can fill the quiet stretches (a rainy Tuesday, a late afternoon) when your dining room is empty but your kitchen is already staffed and open.

In a city like Miami, where tourists in South Beach or Brickell default to whatever app is on their phone and locals order in through the summer heat and storm season, that visibility is worth something. The real question is never "are the apps good or bad," it is "is this reach worth what I am paying," and that depends on the next few sections.

sections.h2: What are the real downsides you have to plan for?
sections.html:
Now the honest costs, beyond the obvious commission. These are the ones that catch owners by surprise.

  • Thin or negative margins. As we saw, a 40 dollar order can shrink to 28 dollars before food cost. If you have not adjusted your prices, some orders can actually lose you money. Volume does not fix a losing unit, it multiplies the loss.
  • You do not own the customer. This is the big one. When someone orders through DoorDash, DoorDash gets their name, email, and phone number. You do not. You cannot text them a Tuesday special or email them a coupon, because you have no way to reach them. You rented a customer for one meal instead of earning one you keep.
  • Dependency. The more of your sales run through the apps, the more power they have over your business. They can change commission rates, tweak how you show up in search, or run promotions that pressure your prices, and you have little say.
  • Errors and refunds you pay for. A driver is late, an item is missing, the food arrives cold. The customer complains to the app, the app issues a refund, and it often comes out of your pocket, even when the driver (not your kitchen) caused it. And that squashed, cold delivery still becomes your restaurant's reputation, even though the app controlled the last mile.

None of this means "never use the apps." It means go in with your eyes open and a plan for each of these, which is exactly what the rest of this guide gives you.

sections.h2: How do you decide if it is worth it for your spot?
sections.html:
Skip the guesswork and run a few honest numbers. You do not need a spreadsheet degree, just five minutes and real figures from your own restaurant.

  1. Find your true food cost on a typical order. Add up what the ingredients cost you. Most restaurants land around 28 to 35 percent of the menu price, so a 40 dollar order runs roughly 12 dollars in food.
  2. Subtract the app's cut. Remove the commission (say 30 percent, or 12 dollars) and processing from that 40 dollar order. Now you are working with about 26 to 28 dollars.
  3. Subtract food and packaging. Take out the 12 dollars of food and a dollar or two of packaging. You are down to roughly 12 to 15 dollars, and you still have not paid your cook or your rent.
  4. Ask the honest question. Is that leftover enough to be worth the kitchen's time on a busy night? Sometimes yes, especially in slow hours. Sometimes the honest answer is that delivery only breaks even, and its job is purely to find you customers you then keep.

Here is a healthy way to think about it. If delivery is profitable on its own, great, run it hard. If it only breaks even, treat it as a marketing cost: you are paying the apps to introduce you to people, and your real profit comes when those people order again directly from you. What you never want is delivery that loses money on every order with no plan to win the customer back. That is the trap.

sections.h2: How do you sign up (and start small)?
sections.html:
If you decide to try it, getting listed is quick. You can be live in a few days. Start on the lowest-commission plan so you are not overpaying while you test, and add only one app at first so you can actually judge the results.

DoorDash

  1. In your web browser, go to merchants.doordash.com and click Sign up or Get started.
  2. Enter your restaurant's basics: business name, address, and phone. Type them exactly as they appear on your Google listing so everything matches.
  3. Choose your plan. You will see the tiered options (basic, plus, premier). Start with the lowest commission tier unless you have a clear reason to pay for more visibility.
  4. Build your menu inside their system, set your hours, and connect a bank account for payouts.
  5. Turn on pickup as well as delivery. Pickup costs you far less, and some customers prefer it.

Uber Eats

  1. Go to merchants.ubereats.com and click Get started (you can also call their merchant line if you would rather talk to a person).
  2. Enter the same exact name, address, and phone you used for DoorDash and Google.
  3. Pick your plan (they use tiers too), and again lean toward the lowest-commission option to begin.
  4. Upload your menu with photos. Good photos genuinely sell more on these apps, so use real, well-lit shots of your actual food.
  5. Set your prep times honestly. If you promise food faster than you can make it, you get bad reviews for being "late."

Whichever you start with, give it a real test window (a month or two), then look at the numbers using the math from the last section before you expand.

sections.h2: How do you make delivery actually profitable?
sections.html:
This is where the winners separate from the strugglers. The apps let you control more than most owners realize. Use every lever.

  • Price your delivery menu higher than dine-in. This is the single biggest fix, and it is completely allowed. Most owners raise app prices by about 10 to 20 percent to cover the commission, so the fee comes out of the app-using customer's order, not your margin. A 12 dollar sandwich might be 14 dollars on the app. The person choosing delivery is already paying for convenience and rarely blinks.
  • Package for the trip, not the counter. Food that arrives soggy or cold triggers refunds and one-star reviews, and both cost you money. Invest in containers that vent steam, seal tightly, and keep hot and cold items apart. Slip in a small card or a coupon for direct ordering (more on that below). Good packaging is cheap insurance.
  • Trim your delivery menu. Not everything travels. Drop or rework dishes that arrive badly, like anything crispy that goes limp. A tighter menu of items that hold up protects your reputation.
  • Push pickup. Pickup commission is a fraction of delivery. Whenever you can nudge a nearby customer to grab their order, you keep far more of it.
  • Use free tools before paid ones. Great photos, accurate hours, and fast prep times lift your ranking for free. Only buy the app's ads or run a discount when you can point to a clear reason (a slow season, a new location), and always check whether the extra orders actually paid off.

Do these five things and delivery goes from a mystery drain to a channel you control.

sections.h2: How do you keep the apps from owning your customers?
sections.html:
Here is the mindset that changes everything: use the apps to get discovered, then win the repeat order on your own turf. The apps are great at introducing you to strangers. They are terrible for you when a loyal regular keeps ordering through them, because you pay a fee on every single order forever.

The goal is to move repeat customers to your own online ordering, where you keep the full amount instead of handing over a cut. This is called commission-free ordering (ordering that runs through your own website, so no marketplace takes a percentage). It is the highest-leverage move in this whole guide. We wrote a full walkthrough on it here: how to set up commission-free online ordering for your restaurant.

A few simple ways to make the switch happen:

  • Put a card in every delivery bag. "Order direct next time and save" with your website address and a small discount. You are literally paying the app to hand you a new customer, so spend a few cents to keep them.
  • Make your website able to take orders. If people who find you on DoorDash try to order from your site and there is no ordering button, they go right back to the app. A modern restaurant site with its own ordering closes that gap. If yours cannot take orders yet, that is worth fixing, and it is exactly what we build (see our restaurant website design).
  • Offer a direct-only perk. A free drink, free delivery over a certain amount, or a loyalty punch that only works when they order from you. Give people a real reason to skip the app next time.

Think of it as a funnel. The apps fill the top with people who never knew you existed. Your job is to catch the good ones and bring them home, where every future order is worth full price. Get that flywheel turning and the commission stops being a wound and becomes what it should be: a fair price for a first introduction.

faqs.q: Is DoorDash worth it for restaurants?
faqs.a: DoorDash can be worth it if you treat it as paid marketing rather than free business. It charges roughly 15 to 30 percent commission per delivery order plus processing, so it is profitable only when you price your delivery menu higher, package food that travels well, and use it to reach new customers you then keep. It is not worth it if you rely on it as your main sales channel and let the fees erase your margin. The smartest approach is to use the app for discovery and move repeat customers to your own commission-free ordering.

faqs.q: How much commission do DoorDash and Uber Eats charge restaurants?
faqs.a: Both charge tiered commission on delivery orders, roughly 15 percent on the basic plan up to about 25 to 30 percent on higher tiers that promise more visibility. On top of that, expect payment processing of about 2.5 to 3.5 percent, and if you buy the apps' optional ads or run discounts, your real cost on those orders can climb toward 30 to 35 percent or more. Pickup orders, where the customer collects the food, cost much less, usually around 6 to 10 percent. These ranges change, so always confirm the current numbers when you sign up.

faqs.q: Should I raise my prices on delivery apps?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is completely allowed. Most restaurants set their delivery-app prices about 10 to 20 percent higher than dine-in to cover the commission the app takes. That way the fee comes out of the convenience-seeking customer's order instead of your margin. A customer choosing delivery is already paying for convenience and rarely notices a modest bump. Keep your dine-in and direct-ordering prices lower so guests have a real reason to come to you instead of the app.

faqs.q: DoorDash or Uber Eats: which should I start with?
faqs.a: Start with whichever app is more popular with your specific customers, then judge it on real numbers rather than reputation. A practical approach is to launch on just one platform, on its lowest-commission plan, and run it for a month or two before deciding whether to add the second. In many US markets DoorDash has the larger share, but Uber Eats can be stronger in dense city areas and with tourists. Starting on one app at a time lets you actually see which one drives profitable orders for your spot.

faqs.q: Do I get my customers' contact information from DoorDash or Uber Eats?
faqs.a: No, and this is one of the biggest drawbacks. When someone orders through a third-party app, the app keeps the customer's name, email, and phone number, not you. That means you cannot email a coupon, text a special, or invite them back on your own. You are essentially renting each customer for a single meal. The fix is to give delivery customers a clear reason to order directly from you next time, so you capture their business on your own website where you keep both the customer and the full order amount.

faqs.q: Is it worth being on both DoorDash and Uber Eats?
faqs.a: It can be, because different customers are loyal to different apps, so being on both widens your reach. But it also doubles the menus, photos, hours, and reviews you have to keep updated, and it splits your data across two systems. A sensible path is to master one app first, confirm delivery is profitable with real numbers, and only add the second once you have the workflow down. Being on both is about reach, not magic, so the same profitability math applies to each one.

faqs.q: How do I get delivery customers to order directly from me instead of the app?
faqs.a: Give them a reason and an easy way to switch. Slip a card into every delivery bag inviting them to order direct for a small discount, offer a perk (a free drink or free delivery) that only works on your own site, and make sure your website can actually take orders so they do not bounce back to the app. This is called commission-free ordering, and it is the single best way to stop paying a fee on repeat customers. Use the apps to get discovered, then win the loyal orders on your own turf.
